1:
The first verb is felt by all to be violent. Ellicott would render it, when we had torn ourselves away; Wesley says it was not without doing violence to both sides; Gill presses it hardest, that the word means they were plucked away, as flesh from the bones or one member from another. Robertson notes it is the verb used of Jesus withdrawing in the garden. Calvin declines the physical sense, referring it not to distance but to the brethren standing on the shore while they could still see the ship. Henry makes it a figure of death, good people being gotten from friends below who would detain them and cannot.

Four stop to describe the ports; Calvin refuses to. The geographers may be consulted about these cities, he says; it is enough for him to show Luke's purpose, which is to let readers weigh the invincible fortitude of a man who would rather be tossed on such winding and troublesome journeys than provide for his own quietness. The others oblige at length. Robertson gives Cos as the birthplace of Hippocrates and Apelles with a great medical school, Rhodes as the island of roses where the sun shone most days, and Patara as having an oracle of Apollo that rivalled Delphi; Ellicott adds the silk of Cos, of fine and almost transparent tissue. On the Colossus, Barnes and Clarke tell one story down to its details, the Saracens after the earthquake selling the prostrate image to a Jew who loaded nine hundred camels with the brass, yet they differ twice on the numbers: Barnes gives fifty-six years standing and a sale about the year six hundred, Clarke sixty-six and six hundred and sixty. Robertson alone draws the point that matters for the voyage: the statue was already lying prostrate when they passed.

The warning at Tyre produces the chapter's first real division, and no two solve it alike. Barnes denies it was a positive command, since had it been, Paul would not have disobeyed it, and reports Grotius rendering it that he should not go unless willing to be bound, with Michaelis and Doddridge to like effect. Clarke says a command from the Spirit would have made Paul highly criminal, and offers Bishop Pearce's reading that the phrase refers to the disciples' own earnestness. Ellicott and Calvin reach one solution independently, that men received the Spirit by measure. Calvin asks whether the Spirit is contrary to himself, loosing Paul whom he held bound inwardly, and answers that those who excel in prophecy may be destitute of judgment; Ellicott says the prophets foresaw the danger but lacked the higher inspiration that guided the Apostle. Robertson puts it shortest: Paul took as information what the disciples gave the form of a prohibition, and duty called louder than warning even when both were the calls of God.

Whether Paul was right divides them further. Ellicott rejects the reading that finds here a self-willed adherence to his own purpose and a chastisement for it in the imprisonment that followed, saying boldly that he was right to go in spite of consequences. Calvin makes the warnings deliberate, sent that by long meditation he might be prepared and his constancy more plainly appear. Clarke draws the opposite moral by a comparison: this was a case like David's at Keilah, and David prevented the threatened evil by leaving while Paul fell into it by going. On the prayer at the water's edge Barnes makes the scene an argument, that no one can read the narrative dispassionately and still believe they used a prescribed form of words; Ellicott and Clarke read it as Jewish custom continued, the beach becoming for the time a place of prayer, Clarke citing Tertullian that they offered their petitions along the shore. Robertson notes from Vincent the first mention of children in the apostolic churches.
7:
Four agree that a clause here is no part of the text. Ellicott says the words answering to Paul's company are wanting in the best manuscripts and seem a needless interpolation, and notes that where they are found some copies put the verb in the third person. Barnes reports it omitted as spurious by Bengel, Griesbach and Knapp and absent from the Syriac and Vulgate; Clarke lists four uncials and four versions against it; Robertson says the best manuscripts omit it. Gill nevertheless expounds it as genuine and names the company, Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Timothy, Tychicus, Trophimus and Luke; and Henry builds a reflection on it, that as those who sailed together parted when the voyage ended, so those who travel together through this world separate at death, and then it appears who are of Paul's company and who are not.

On the port they disagree about its present state. Barnes describes a living city, besieged in the crusades, taken by Bonaparte, surrendered to the British fleet under Admiral Stopford after a few hours' resistance, and holding some twenty thousand people. Wesley says it is now, like many other once noble cities, only a heap of ruins. Ellicott traces the names instead: Accho of the book of Judges was rebuilt and renamed by Ptolemy Soter, the old name revived or was never wholly disused, and the natives still say Accho while Europeans know it as Acre. Robertson adds that it was never taken by Israel, was reckoned Philistine by the Hebrews and Phoenician by the Greeks, and had the best harbour on the coast.

Philip's title starts an argument about office. Barnes reasons that since the word is applied to him and to none of the other six, he must have had a special commission to preach, which does not belong to a deacon, whose business was to care for the poor. Calvin infers something larger, that the deaconship continued only for a time, since it would not otherwise have been lawful for Philip to leave Jerusalem; and he places evangelists between apostles and doctors, next to the apostles in function though inferior in honour, free to preach everywhere without a fixed station. Ellicott says the serving of tables had been merged in the higher work, so that Philip was no longer known as a deacon if he ever had been. Robertson calls this the earliest of the word's three uses in the New Testament, guesses it was coined of Philip as the Baptist's title was of John, and reports it from an inscription of uncertain date.

Two see Luke gathering material here. Ellicott imagines the historian, meeting Philip for the first time and already contemplating his work, asking many questions and learning all or nearly all that stands in the first eleven chapters of this book; Robertson supposes Luke did take notes from Philip and his daughters about the beginnings of Christian history, and calls these precious days for him. On the four daughters five positions appear. Ellicott makes them a class answering to the widows, cites the catacomb inscriptions and Pliny's letter to Trajan, and holds that Paul was open to the teachings of experience here and modified his judgment later; the very prohibition of women speaking, he adds, proves the practice was common. Robertson finds the prohibitions hard to reconcile with the permission elsewhere and wonders whether Paul knew local conditions he has not told, adding that the problem calls for restraint and reverence. Calvin, holding that women bear no public office, concludes they prophesied at home or in private. Clarke supposes they were no more than teachers, and asks why, if they might be prophetesses, they might not teach. Gill takes from the verse only that Philip was a married man, which he observes against those who forbid marriage to the clergy.
10:
The girdle is read by all as prophecy in the old manner, and each supplies precedents. Ellicott calls it a revival of predicting by symbolic acts and instances Isaiah walking naked and barefoot, Jeremiah leaving his girdle by the Euphrates and wearing yokes, and Ezekiel portraying the siege on a tile. Barnes and Clarke give the same roll, Barnes adding the potter. Robertson alone carries it forward instead of back, noting that Jesus interpreted the symbolism of Peter girding himself. Calvin alone notes the counterfeit: such signs might seem toys to the common sort, but the Spirit who applied them touched the godly inwardly, and afterwards the false prophets tried the same policy, since Satan is in a manner God's ape, Zedekiah making himself horns and Ananias breaking Jeremiah's yoke. Ellicott and Robertson both prefer the reading by which Agabus bound his own hands rather than Paul's.

Why a fourth warning was needed at all is answered differently. Calvin says Paul had been more than sufficiently admonished already, so that this was added for other men's sake, that they might know he entered the combat willingly and was appointed of God a champion for the gospel. Wesley says simply that the nearer the event, the more express the predictions that prepared him for it. Ellicott looks to the man rather than the message, supposing that Agabus, knowing the feeling at Jerusalem, came down in friendly anxiety to warn him not to come. Robertson notes that the word for delivering is the one Jesus used of himself, and that Paul was indeed delivered into Gentile hands and took five years to get free.

Whether the prophecy bound Paul splits the two Wesleyan voices against each other. Clarke says they all understood it to be conditional and contingent, that it was in Paul's power to turn the scale, and that everyone saw he had power to go or not to go. Wesley says the exact reverse, that Paul knew this prediction had the force of a command and that they did not know it. Ellicott reconstructs the proposal they were pressing, that those less known and so in less danger might go up without him, pay the collected fund over to James and the elders, and return to him at Caesarea; and Luke, he notes, admits joining the entreaty himself.

Two of them reach for the same modern parallel at the refusal. Ellicott says it was with no Stoic hardness that Paul resisted, that the entreaties were positively crushing and he adhered to his purpose as with a broken heart, yet his martyr-like and Luther-like nature carried him forward. Robertson gets there by anecdote, citing Regulus returning from Rome to Carthage and Luther answering Spalatin that though the devils in Worms were as many as tiles upon the roofs, thither would he go; Paul's readiness, he adds, is like that of Jesus setting his face to go to Jerusalem. On the words with which the company gave way, four readings appear. Barnes takes them for true piety, the friends now assured that it was God's will and ready to submit. Calvin says they yielded lest they resist the Holy Spirit, by whom they understood Paul to be governed. Ellicott thinks it too much to find here any acceptance of his purpose as the Lord's will, calling the words resignation to what was seen to be inevitable and possibly a quotation from the prayer the Lord taught. Robertson is sharper, finding a quaint naivete in the confession: since Paul would not let them have their way, they were willing for the Lord to have his, which is acquiescence after failure. Gill notes only that the weeping distressed the apostle more than the prophecy had.
15:
An obsolete English word occupies four of them. Barnes calls the rendering carriages a most unhappy translation, since the word now means only the vehicle and once meant the thing carried, and he cites David leaving his baggage with the keeper of it. Ellicott gives the same instance and adds Udal's version of Erasmus, where the bearers of the paralytic take their heavy carriage to the house-roof. Clarke says shortly that they packed up their things and got their baggage in order, which is what the text means. Wesley adds that the heavier luggage had probably gone by sea already and that what they carried now was the alms for Jerusalem. Robertson reports Ramsay's view that the verb means to saddle horses. Henry has them serving as their own porters, so little had they of change of raiment.

Where Mnason was met is disputed on three readings. Barnes holds the sentence better rendered that they were brought to Mnason, who lived at Jerusalem and did not travel with them. Clarke thinks it unlikely they would bring along the man in whose house they were to lodge and prefers Bishop Patrick's rendering, though he allows Mnason may have come down to Caesarea and returned with them. Robertson supplies a third from Codex Bezae, which adds the words to a certain village and so makes the lodging a house about halfway up, and he judges that this may be true. Gill simply has him travelling in the party.

What made him an old disciple is answered four ways. Ellicott prefers early to old, holding the word refers less to personal age than to his having been a disciple from the beginning, and suggests he may have been among the men of Cyprus who first preached to Gentiles at Antioch. He goes further and makes him one of Luke's own informants, of those who had been from the beginning eye-witnesses and ministers of the word, and finds it interesting as showing that the Lord's disciples were not limited to natives of Galilee and Judea. Barnes guesses at a convert made before the crucifixion; Clarke offers either an early convert, probably one of those at Pentecost, or simply a man now old; Henry reports the opinion that he was one of the seventy, and praises the honour of continuing long in a course of duty to a good old age. Robertson quotes Furneaux that as the number of the first disciples lessened, the next generation accorded a sort of honour to the survivors.

Ellicott alone reads the lodging as a precaution. The arrangement seems to him the best course that could be taken to minimise the danger the Apostle was running: in that house he might at least be sure of personal safety, and the men who came from Caesarea would form a kind of escort as he moved about the city. Calvin instead praises those companions, who having been repulsed do not refuse to share the danger, though it would have been a plausible excuse that no law bound them to be hauled to death through one man's stubbornness. On the welcome itself Barnes reads plain joy at a safe return from distant regions and many dangers; Ellicott and Robertson both take it as informal and private, given by personal friends in Mnason's house before the formal reception next day; and Calvin makes it a lesson against rumour, that James and his fellows in office, being well persuaded of Paul's uprightness, were not estranged from him by the daily efforts of envious men, and that we must shut our ears against false reports, since Satan knows nothing is fitter to lay waste the kingdom of Christ than discord among the faithful. Gill uses the verse to catalogue the later bishops of Caesarea from Reland, down to the councils of Chalcedon.
18:
The one name given raises a question about the rest, and two answer alike across thirteen centuries. Calvin conjectures that the other apostles had gone into diverse places to preach as their calling required, and that they so divided themselves that James stood still at Jerusalem, whither strangers daily resorted, which was all one as if he had preached far and wide in remote places. Robertson notices that the apostles are not mentioned though both were named at the earlier council, and infers that they are away on preaching tours. On the title, Chrysostom calls James the Bishop of Jerusalem without hesitation and Clarke follows him, while Ellicott gives it with a caveat, that it expresses his functions though apparently not then borne by him, and Robertson will say only that he is clearly the leading elder. Wesley calls him the Lord's brother and the only apostle then presiding in Judea, and says Paul went in with the company that they might appear all of one mind.

Why the elders met without the church is explained twice over. Calvin says that whenever weighty business was handled the elders came together, that the consultation might be quieter without the multitude, the people being admitted afterwards. Robertson supposes instead that the church was not called because of the known prejudice against Paul created by the Judaizers. Robertson observes that Luke is present, and that the fullness of the report here and at Caesarea reads like an eyewitness story. Gill records only that the salute was given by a kiss, as the Arabic version adds, or by asking after their health.

How Paul was received at this formal meeting divides them flatly. Ellicott says there was no reluctance on their part to receive the Apostle of the Gentiles into full fellowship, and that Luke is careful to add that they were all there. Robertson raises the opposite possibility, that Paul may have observed an absence of warmth in contrast with the welcome of his friends the day before, and quotes Furneaux that his misgiving about the collection looks to have been confirmed, and that we never hear of the Jerusalem Christians putting in a word for him with either authority or expressing sympathy during his long imprisonment. Robertson grants only that the Judaizers did not appear actively against him, and that the collection and the plan proposed stopped the mouths of those lions. Calvin and Henry read the scene as free from envy, the elders glorifying God for the success of a man honoured above them.

Chrysostom hears embarrassment where the others hear counsel. He marks the unassuming behaviour of James, who does not discourse authoritatively as bishop but takes Paul as partner in their view; he finds them apologising at the outset, as if to say they did not wish this and Paul should see the necessity of the thing; and they do not say how many thousands they have made catechumens, but only that there are so many. They advise rather than command, he adds, and ask a defence made in act and not in word. On Paul's part he says the Apostle did not plead that he could produce Timothy whom he had circumcised, or satisfy them by argument, but complied and did all, since so it was expedient, his bearing the expenses being a step open to no suspicion. Against this stands Henry, who says the apostles were not free from blame in all they did, that it would be hard to defend Paul from the charge of giving way too much, and that integrity is more likely to preserve us than insincere compliances. Barnes and Clarke take the narrative itself as the answer to prejudice, since God would not have made a bad man so singular an instrument of good; Ellicott notes it must have been long, ending with the contribution from well-nigh all the Gentile churches.
20:
The number is felt to be large and defended three ways. Ellicott says the word is literally myriads, and that though the figure seems great for Jerusalem the pilgrim crowds would justify it; Clarke likewise refuses to confine it to the city. Robertson calls it surprising even as hyperbole and adds that we need not count the hostile Jews from Asia, who were not Christians at all. Barnes traces a line from the three thousand of Pentecost onward, arguing the work then begun had never ceased. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the next word is a substantive, so that they were zealots for the law, an almost technical term for the most rigid Pharisees; Robertson adds that a party of Zealots grew out of the Pharisees and brought on the war with Rome, and that one of the twelve bore the name.

Whether the report about Paul was true is the sharpest division in the chapter, and it splits the two Wesleyan voices. Clarke says the information was incorrect, that we do not find Paul preaching thus, and that though he had shown circumcision unavailing he never told a Jew to forsake Moses, the ceremonies being useless but not destructive, and dangerous only when depended on for salvation. Barnes calls the report slanderous, a perversion of what Paul really argued; Robertson says the elders themselves did not believe it but wished Paul to set it straight. Wesley says flatly that the charge was true, that Paul did so teach and so wrote to the Galatians, and breaks out that James himself had assented to Peter that this law was a yoke neither their fathers nor they could bear, marvelling that they did not know it, or knowing it did not testify it at all hazards to every Jewish convert in Jerusalem.

Ellicott takes a middle course and concedes more than the rest. As a personal accusation, he says, it was easy to refute, since Paul was to the Jews as a Jew, had taken a vow himself and circumcised Timothy, and it was probably false that he ever taught Jews not to circumcise their children. But fanaticism is sometimes clear-sighted in its bitterness, he adds, and the Judaisers felt that once circumcision was proclaimed nothing it ceased to have any reason for existing and sank to a badge of the national exclusiveness which Paul's teaching was itself demolishing. If a Jew had asked why he should then circumcise his child, no satisfying answer was easy: the plea of avoiding offence was temporary, and the plea of a divine command met the reply that the seal had lost its force when the covenant was superseded. Few Christians now, he observes, would hold a converted Jew bound to circumcise as well as baptise his children.

What the crowd's gathering means divides them once more. Barnes takes it as an inevitable tumult friendship required them to try to prevent; Clarke will not say whether a convocation or a riot is meant, but sees the elders forestalling an evil they had reason to fear; Wesley expects a tumult unless the people are pacified. Calvin reads the necessity the other way: it would have been absurd for an apostle of such report not to come before the whole multitude of the faithful, since shunning the sight of the people would only have deepened suspicion. He praises the elders for preventing the offence in time, though allowing that in requiring a vow they bore perhaps too indulgently with the people's infirmity. Robertson notes that two uncials and several cursives omit the clause. Clarke accounts for the tangle providentially, that God tolerated the Mosaic dispensation until the destruction of Jerusalem made its observance impossible. Gill reads the opening question as asking both whether the report is true and what is to be done.
23:
The mechanics are supplied by three, with one authority cited twice. Ellicott notes that the minimum term was thirty days, which Paul could not now complete, but that usage let a man attach himself to a company of Nazarites for the final seven days of purification, shaving and sacrificing with them, a devout act especially if he paid for the offerings; and he cites Agrippa as gaining credit this way. Clarke cites the same passage of Josephus through Bishop Pearce, that Agrippa had many Nazarites shaven and furnished the money. Robertson quotes Page that it was reckoned a work of piety to relieve needy Jews of the expense, and reports Ramsay's view that Paul had command of money at this period, perhaps from his father's estate, since a poor man, as Furneaux says, would not have been treated with the respect paid him at Caesarea and at Rome.

Ellicott alone observes who gave the advice, quoting Hegesippus that James himself lived under the Nazarite rule, no razor coming upon his head and he drinking neither wine nor strong drink, so that in joining such a vow Paul showed himself content to follow him. He finds it interesting that the four were members of the Jerusalem church, as showing how intensely Jewish that church still was. Calvin takes the opposite view of the same four, that though reckoned among the faithful their vow was superstitious, and that the elders had fallen into a foolish indulgence through too much love of their nation.

Whether Paul should have complied opens the widest division in the chapter. Wesley condemns it, asking whether Paul could follow such advice in godly sincerity and whether the yielding was not too great a deference to mere men; Paul ought, he says, to have answered plainly that he did not keep the Mosaic law and none of them need keep it, since Peter did not and God had commanded him not to; and he calls it a yielding to counsel that flowed not from spiritual but carnal wisdom. Clarke, of the same school, confesses it exceedingly difficult to account for the conduct of James, the elders and Paul; he sets out the charge that some have censured it as the greatest error of Paul's life and a virtual denial of Christ, and that his long trouble beginning immediately after has been read as a judgment for it. His answer is that one cannot wonder enough that so wise a man should be guilty of it and all the elders advise it, that no sacred writer ever censured the act, and that Paul himself, elsewhere so ready to own his failings, reflects on it with comfort.

The rest defend him on different grounds. Barnes meets the charge of double-dealing in four steps: the law was not necessary to justification, was never enjoined on Gentile converts, was opposed by Paul wherever urged as necessary to salvation, and was here conformed to as missionaries always conform to innocent customs. Calvin denies that Paul dissembled, holding that he sincerely professed not to hate the law, while granting it was not profitable that he be long counted an observer of it; he allows the charge of his being too easily entreated some colour, refuses the claim that his troubles were punishment, and turns the example against the false Nicodemites who plead it to cover their dissimulation. Robertson answers Furneaux, who calls the act a compromise and a failure, that this obscures a complex situation: the aim was not to conciliate the Judaizers but to break their power over the thousands they had deluded, and that was accomplished, the explosion which followed coming from other enemies. Ellicott says only that all promised well until an interruption came from an unexpected quarter, and Gill that Paul would readily condescend in such a case yet stiffly opposed the same things whenever pressed as necessary to salvation.
27:
When in the seven days the seizure fell is disputed. Barnes denies that the Greek means almost ended, and concludes with Doddridge, from later dates, that the arrest fell near the beginning of them; Wesley agrees. Ellicott and Robertson put it at the end, Robertson saying it was on the last day, while the offerings for all five were being completed, that the incident occurred which made Paul a prisoner for five years. What the days are Ellicott settles negatively: not the vow, never less than thirty days, nor the feast, never beyond one, but the special purification at the final stage. Gill reports the Syriac reading of the seventh day, and the opinion that the seven weeks to Pentecost are meant.

On the barrier the commentary tradition is overtaken by a spade. Clarke, having only Josephus, reports an inscription in Greek and Latin on the wall dividing the courts, warning that no stranger might come within on pain of death, and argues that with such a prohibition before his eyes Paul would hardly have entered with an uncircumcised Greek, so that the calumny refutes itself. Ellicott and Robertson can point to the stone: both cite the slab found and deciphered by Clermont-Ganneau in eighteen seventy-one, Robertson noting it had been built into the wall of a mosque on the Via Dolorosa. Ellicott gives its text, that no man of alien race is to enter within the balustrade round the temple, and that any one taken in the act has himself to blame for the death that follows.

Two notice that the charge is Stephen's returned. Ellicott says they bring against Paul in almost identical terms the accusation he had once brought against Stephen, and so make themselves witnesses of it; Robertson notes the likeness and Paul's confessed part in it. Robertson then weighs it: truth and falsehood are mixed, for Paul had said that being a Jew would not save a man, that the law did not bind Gentiles, and that the temple was not the only place to worship God, yet he gloried in being a Jew and was honouring the temple at that moment. On the specific charge Clarke calls it a malicious untruth, the sight of Trophimus with him in the city being no ground for a slander that must cost lives; Robertson calls it false, made of inferences of hate; Calvin says the accusers betray by such lightness how venomous they were.

Robertson traces the mob to Ephesus. Paul was by now unknown by face to many Jerusalem Jews, though once the leader of the persecution, but the Jews of Ephesus knew him too well and some were at the feast; the verb for stirring up the crowd is the one used of the riot there, learned, he says, from Demetrius the silversmith, and he guesses the cry was led by the Alexander those Jews had put forward. Having raised it, these enemies vanish completely. He notes the irony that in the act of honouring the temple Paul is accused of dishonouring it, and that the word shouted means to run at a cry, as though murder had been done. Henry presses the same irony, that in the temple where he should have been protected as in a sanctuary he was set upon by men who would have had his blood mingled with his sacrifices, and that the church is polluted by none more than persecutors acting under colour of her name. Calvin draws a lesson instead, that while Paul is bent on pacifying the faithful he incurs the rage of the enemies, and that we must not take it impatiently when counsels formed with a right affection fall out ill. Barnes allows that Paul may indeed have declared the temple would be destroyed; Gill wonders why so loud a call for help was needed against one man, little of stature and weak in body.
29:
Luke's parenthesis exposes a bad inference, and two make a moral of it. Barnes calls it a striking illustration of the way accusations are brought: they had seen Trophimus with Paul in the city and inferred that he had been with him in the temple, not even pretending to have seen it; if men would state facts as they are, no small part of the slander in the world would cease. Robertson lays out the same fallacy, that the men had two facts and put their inference on the same footing with them, adding that this is the way of the mob-mind in all ages, many an innocent man having been rushed to death by a lynching party. Ellicott puts it shortest, that hatred added wings to imagination.

Why the doors were shut behind him is answered four ways. Ellicott says it was plainly the act of the Levite gate-keepers, guarding the precincts against further profanation. Robertson agrees the Levites shut them, but gives the crowd's reason, that they did not wish to defile the holy place with blood. Clarke reverses the motive: they were shut to keep Paul from succour and to allow an unmolested killing in the outer court, reckoned less holy. Wesley adds a third purpose, to prevent his taking sanctuary at the horns of the altar; and he notes the rule that any uncircumcised person entering the inner temple might be stoned without further process, which the crowd thought they were executing.

The fortress is described from Josephus by two in the same terms: Hyrcanus built it and called it Baris, Herod beautified it and named it for Mark Antony, and it had four towers, one overlooking the temple. Clarke adds Josephus's summary, that as the temple was a guard to the city so this castle guarded the temple, and Bishop Pearce's inference from the porticoes that the attempted killing was in the court of the Gentiles. Ellicott places it at the north-west angle with two flights of stairs to the arcades, the garrison being there to command the pilgrim crowds while the Procurator was away at Caesarea. Calvin corrects the title, saying Luke calls him tribune of the band improperly, since such an officer was set over a thousand, as the mention of centurions shows; Robertson adds that ten years earlier a Roman guard had marched down in a passover riot and several hundred were trampled to death.

Calvin presses the deliverance hardest. The tribune, he says, thought of no such thing but came only to quiet a tumult, so that the Lord showed the plainer token of his providence in delivering Paul without man's counsel, suffering the faithful to be almost oppressed that he may rescue them the more wonderfully; unbelievers would call it fortune, but the Spirit has painted providence reigning amid the confused uproars of men. He notes with contempt that men whom neither the majesty of God nor the reverence of the temple could stay began to relent at the sight of a profane soldier, which shows they were fired by cruelty rather than zeal; and he commends the tribune's equity by comparison, since he chains Paul as an evil-doer yet vouchsafes to hear him, where the others beat him unmercifully. Ellicott says only that the Apostle again owed his safety to the civil power. On the chains, Barnes and Ellicott agree he was fastened between two soldiers, Barnes adding that this showed the crowd justice was not being cheated, while Robertson takes it as the treatment of a seditious man. Barnes and Wesley both note that the prophecy of Agabus was thus fulfilled, Wesley observing that it was fulfilled by Roman hands, and counting the ends of providence answered by the imprisonment, which preserved Paul's life after he had suffered severely for worldly prudence. Gill notes only that they had seen Trophimus with him in Jerusalem, not Ephesus.
35:
The cry from the stairs is recognised by four. Ellicott, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all note that away with him was the shout raised at the Crucifixion, Clarke adding that in a Jewish mob's mouth it always means kill him. Robertson observes that Paul will hear it again, that Luke does not say they demanded crucifixion, and that Paul was learning what it was to share the sufferings of Christ as the sullen roar rolled on in his ears. Ellicott and Barnes describe the press as so great that the soldiers had to lift him from his feet, Barnes and Wesley quoting the tower's rock of fifty cubits with stairs to the porticoes, Gill citing Aristeas.

Why the tribune was surprised is neatly put by Ellicott: the officer expected Aramaic and was startled by Greek, the people expected Greek and were startled by Aramaic, and nothing could better illustrate how familiar Jerusalem was with both. Barnes and Clarke both infer from his buying his citizenship with a great sum that he was no Roman by birth, Barnes thinking Greek was his own tongue and Clarke that his Latin was imperfect. Calvin takes the request as duty: Paul offered to defend his cause as all God's servants must, since we are bound to make our integrity known lest through our infamy God's name be blasphemed.

The question about the Egyptian turns on a particle. Ellicott says the Greek has an illative wanting in the English, so that it reads, art not thou then that Egyptian, the guess being drawn from the prisoner's Greek; he reports the alternative, thou art not then that Egyptian, as though the Greek had changed the officer's mind, and objects that an Egyptian Jew from the land of the Septuagint would naturally speak Greek. Robertson takes the reading Ellicott rejects. Calvin adds a refutation nobody else offers, that the man meant is not Theudas, since Theudas carried away only four hundred, the captain reckons four thousand and calls them murderers, and Theudas rose under an earlier emperor.

On the numbers the discrepancy with Josephus is met four ways, and Gill supplies its cause by reporting that Josephus gives both figures himself, four hundred killed and two hundred taken in one place, thirty thousand gathered in another. Ellicott dismisses the larger, such statistics being never to be relied on; Robertson suggests Lysias means only the armed core of the mob; Clarke offers a harmony, that six and twenty thousand had melted away before Olivet, and reports Dean Aldridge's conjecture that copyists mistook the Greek letter for four and wrote thirty thousand, supported by the disproportion of six hundred casualties to so great a host. Barnes turns the difficulty round, finding a mark of truth in the fact that neither historian names the Egyptian. Tarsus is defended with the same two authorities twice, Barnes and Clarke citing Xenophon for a great and flourishing city and Josephus for the metropolis of the Cilicians, Clarke adding Ammianus and Ellicott the coins calling it an independent metropolis. Chrysostom reads the exchange as tactics: Paul does not decline the aids afforded by the laws but awes the tribune with the name of his city, and in owning himself a Jew did not deny being a Christian. He marks the providence, that unless the tribune had come and bound him Paul would neither have wished to speak nor obtained silence, and asks what spectacle could equal a man in two chains haranguing the people; Robertson calls the moment heroic, recalling that his enemies had said his bodily presence was weak and his speech contemptible. Ellicott closes by noting that many there had not seen Paul act in public since the day, twenty-five years before, when he kept the garments of Stephen's murderers. Clarke and Barnes both complain that the chapter is divided unnaturally, Clarke noting that it ends at a comma.
